title: Why doesn't the Moon fall to Earth?
subtitle: Orbit & gravity
subject: sciences
description: The Moon is falling toward the Earth all the time. It simply misses, every single time. That is exactly what an orbit is.

hero.hook: The Moon is falling toward us. It just misses the Earth on every lap.

blocks.text: If the Earth's gravity pulls on the Moon, why does it not crash into us? The answer sounds odd: the Moon really is **falling** toward the Earth. It just misses, at every moment.

That balance between falling and moving sideways is an **orbit**, a curved path around a body. The English physicist **Isaac Newton** was the first to explain a falling apple and the motion of the planets with one and the same idea.
If you weighed **60 kg** on Earth, you would weigh only about **10** on the Moon: its gravity is six times weaker.
Newton pictured a cannon on top of a mountain so high that it rose above the atmosphere. Fire a cannonball horizontally. With little power, it soon falls back. With more force, it travels farther.

blocks.caption: Newton's cannonball thought experiment: the key to understanding an orbit

blocks.text: At one precise speed, called [[Orbital velocity]], something remarkable happens. While the ball falls, the Earth, which is round, curves away beneath it at the same rate. The ball keeps falling and never touches the ground. It is in **permanent free fall**, pulled by gravity without ever crashing.
The Moon does the same thing. It has enough sideways speed to turn a fall into a loop. Without that speed, it would drop straight onto us.

The Moon orbits at about **384,000 km**. Its sideways speed is roughly **1 km/s**. If it stopped dead, it would crash into us within days. If gravity vanished all at once, it would fly off in a straight line into space, following the principle of [[Inertia]]: a body keeps its speed unless something slows it down.

[[Newton's law of universal gravitation]] says that every mass attracts every other mass, and that the pull weakens with distance, more precisely with the square of the distance. The closer a satellite is, the faster it has to travel to avoid falling.
The International Space Station, only **400 km** up, races along at about **28,000 km/h**. It circles the Earth in **90 minutes**. The Moon, much farther out, takes **27.3 days**.
So an orbit is not magic. It is a constant compromise between “I am falling” and “I am moving too fast to hit anything.”

sections.title: The tides push the Moon away

blocks.text: The orbit is not fixed. [[Tidal forces]] come into play. The Moon's gravity pulls harder on the side of the Earth facing it than on the center. It deforms the oceans and raises a bulge of water.

Because the Earth spins on itself faster than the Moon travels around it, that bulge runs slightly ahead of the Moon. Friction slows the Earth's rotation very slightly: our days grow longer by about **1.4 milliseconds** per century. In exchange, the Moon drifts away by about **3.8 cm** a year.

Billions of years ago, the Moon was far closer. The tides were enormous. That churning of water and chemistry may have helped the first forms of life. And the dinosaurs lived on an Earth where a day lasted only **22 or 23 hours**.

Today, by a geometric coincidence, the Sun is about **400 times** bigger than the Moon, but also **400 times** farther away. The two therefore have the same **apparent size**, the angle they cover in our sky. That is what makes total solar eclipses possible.

In about **600 million years**, the Moon will be too far away to hide the Sun completely. Only annular eclipses will remain: a ring of light around the lunar disk. In the very long run, the Earth and the Moon could lock together, each always showing the same face to the other. But the Sun, turning into a **red giant**, the final phase of a star like ours, will transform the system long before that.
The Moon does not crash because its sideways speed balances the Earth's pull: it is in permanent free fall. And it is still drifting away by about **3.8 cm** a year.
